title: Second-line era musicians and Eddie Jackson on bass horn
summary: Joseph remembers old brass band players such as George Washington and Willie Humphrey, and Eddie Jackson's powerful bass.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from

blocks.x: Because I had just... I had someone else to service. Yeah. Because I remember that good, you see. Because I got the service. And at that time, he couldn't put off civilian clothes. He still had to do in the uniform. He couldn't see. It's not like this today. You can change the clothes. You can see where you can go. And I went... I thought I could get from... I came here. Looking around the left. My dad... I got my advice to my brother. I know where. I was in the place where... He wasn't... They run the hell out of me. They didn't lie. So he said that.
Yeah, Bill. In the first time, they see my cousin... Another man too, I didn't tell you about. You see, man, your parents?
Yeah. I never... I met him. I never...
That was another... That was a man.
Bill, that man... You can get that man from Canal and Ramport to Lidenfield.

He know how he looked like a little Mexican. He was bigger than me. Short. Just like me. But he's heavenly to me. And I used to like the other man to play the trumpet. I used to say... That time... I was talking about second line prayer. I used to like second line prayer by them kind of fellas. But that time, they had old George Washington. Do you ever know where the George Washington... Trombone? Trombone play. He's about that like. About that big. I never saw him, though. That big. And that same Willie Humphrey, Daddy, used to play a sax. Daddy, used to put a saxophone, stripes on him. He don't like to hook up a horse. Put on his stripes, all around his buddy. He had a big buddy. Old man. Yeah, we interviewed him. Yeah. Well, you know... And man, I think it kicks out all that. Boy, them old fellas, boy, see, in that time, they had the... And Pete, Pete Buckeye used to play with them, too, from Cross the River. You know Pete. Yeah, sure. He was living there. Pete was with all them old man. And I said, I tell you, I really enjoyed that music them fellas used to play them old fellas.

To see the different music. See, that fella used to play for Red. That fella didn't look like they was tired. Billy, they didn't look like they was tired. They didn't get tired. No, they didn't get tired. And they had a bass horn player they called Eddie Jackson. You know what I mean?
I heard of him. I never got to hear him, though.
Bam. That's a man you can yearn from Cross the River to the North Eastern.
But I've heard he had a powerful tone.

Man, he was powerful. He was powerful. And everybody liked him. Every musician in town liked him. Every musician in the world had something good to see about him. And Bill, you know what kind of fool he was? About this big. Real strong. I like that. He was tall.
That's right. I saw a picture of him.
Yeah. He was a skinny man. A skinny, big, tall man. He wouldn't take a man and blow a horn like that. No,
